notes.title: The P sweep: separate runs, one per yardstick
notes.body:
P fixes the yardstick the ratio is measured against. Each run constrains the
search to demands the optimal routes at exactly MLU = P; the whole search is
then re-run for several values of P, and the largest ratio found wins. So it is
a sweep of separate searches, not one search that also optimizes P.

Why it is needed: it is the fallback for DOTE possibly NOT being scale-
invariant. MLU(d,f) is homogeneous -- scaling every demand by k scales every
utilization by k -- so MLU_OPT(k*d) = k*MLU_OPT(d), and every demand can be
scaled onto the MLU_OPT = 1 surface. If DOTE's split ratios are unchanged by
that scaling, MLU_DOTE is homogeneous too, the ratio is constant along each ray
from the origin, and the single cross-section P = 1 already covers every
direction -- which is exactly why they say P = 1 is sufficient for MLU. A DNN
has no built-in reason to be scale-invariant, though; when it is not, the ratio
varies along a ray, one cross-section is no longer the whole search space, and
sweeping P restores the magnitude dimension that normalizing threw away.
notes.quote: We then search for the value of P that results in the largest performance ratio. Our method is fast (5), so we can run it multiple times. For MLU, solving for P = 1 is sufficient.

notes.title: Eq. (1) alone still needs the whole model
notes.body:
Eq. (1) as written, x <- x + alpha * grad_x M_adv(H(x)), hides a demand: to take
that gradient you need H -- the entire pipeline, DNN plus post-processor plus
routing plus MLU -- as one symbolic expression you can differentiate. That is
the same thing MetaOpt asks for when it wants the system as an MILP. So Eq. (1)
on its own buys you nothing: you have swapped a solver that needs the whole
model for a gradient that needs the whole model.

The escape is the next paragraph and Figure 4: you never need H itself, only the
chain rule over its pieces. Each H_i is differentiated in place -- autograd
through a DNN, a hand-derived formula, or a numerical estimate from samples --
and the Jacobians are multiplied, so no single expression describing the
composition ever exists.
notes.quote: Equation (1) still requires modeling a complex learning-enabled system as a closed form expression H (x), which goes against our initial goal for an easy-to-use gray-box solution.

notes.title: "Mathematical representation" is weaker than "exact model"
notes.body:
Two routes to the same Jacobian, and "mathematical representation" is doing
careful work here: it is deliberately weaker than "exact model".

1. Mathematical representation. You know the component's formula well enough to
   differentiate it -- nothing more. The routing step is linear,
   loads = pte^T (f * d), so its Jacobian is exactly pte^T. For the DNN,
   autograd is the mechanical version of the same thing.

   The contrast is with what a white-box tool needs: the function re-expressed
   in the solver's restricted algebra (linear constraints, MILP, first-order
   logic), globally valid, and encoded jointly with every other component. That
   is why MetaOpt needed DOTE's activation swapped for a piecewise-linear one --
   not because the true activation has no derivative, but because it could not
   be written in the solver's language. A tanh has a perfectly good mathematical
   representation and a trivial derivative; it simply is not MILP-encodable.
   So "representation" means differentiable form, not solver-encodable form.

2. Samples. When the formula is not available at all -- a closed-source
   component, a simulator, a measurement -- probe it at nearby inputs and
   estimate the gradient numerically. Citation [39] is a Gaussian process
   regression tutorial, so the intent is fitting a local surrogate and
   differentiating that, rather than raw finite differences.

The difference that matters: route 1 gives the exact Jacobian, route 2 an
approximation -- which is where Section 6's hedge "(approximately) piecewise
sub-differentiable" comes from.

In our reimplementation everything went through route 1 (DNN by autograd,
routing and the max analytically). Route 2 is never exercised, which is a soft
spot in the paper: it carries real weight in the generality claim but is
demonstrated nowhere.
notes.quote: We do not need an exact model of each function Hi to compute the gradients. We can either compute the gradient through its mathematical representation or compute it locally through samples of the function [39].
